nodes.summary: A group $G$ is left-orderable if it admits a linear order $\le$ such that $a \le b$ implies $ca \le cb$ for all $a, b, c \in G$.
nodes.title: Left-orderable groups

nodes.summary: There exists a group $G$ that has unique products but is not left-orderable: for all finite nonempty subsets $X, Y \subseteq G$ there are $x_0 \in X$ and $y_0 \in Y$ such that $(x_0, y_0)$ is the only pair $(x, y) \in X \times Y$ with $xy = x_0 y_0$, and yet $G$ admits no linear order invariant under left multiplication.
nodes.title: A unique product group need not be left-orderable

nodes.summary: The statement, asked by P. Linnell, that there exists a group $G$ with unique products that is not left-orderable. Here $G$ has unique products if for all finite nonempty subsets $X, Y \subseteq G$ there are $x_0 \in X$ and $y_0 \in Y$ such that $(x_0, y_0)$ is the only pair $(x, y) \in X \times Y$ with $xy = x_0 y_0$.
nodes.title: Kourovka Problem 15.49 (unique product groups and left orders)
